column2: The set Ω of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
A subset of the sample space: a set of outcomes to which we can assign a probability.
Events A and B are independent if P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B); learning that one occurred does not change the probability of the other.
P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) (for P(B) > 0): the probability of A given that B has occurred.
If B1,…,Bk partition the sample space, then P(A) = Σ_i P(A|Bi)P(Bi).
P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). For a partition: P(Ai|B) = P(B|Ai)P(Ai) / Σ_j P(B|Aj)P(Aj).

A function X that maps each outcome in the sample space to a real number, so we can talk about probabilities of numerical events such as {X ≤ x}. Used to model uncertain quantities such as data, measurements or parameters.
F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x). Non-decreasing, right-continuous, going from 0 to 1; defined for both discrete and continuous variables.
For a discrete random variable, f_X(x) = P(X = x).
For a continuous random variable, a function f with P(a < X < b) = ∫_a^b f(x)dx; it is the derivative of the CDF. f(x) itself is not a probability.
Standard parametric families used as building blocks. Discrete: Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Geometric, Categorical. Continuous: Uniform, Normal, Exponential, Gamma, Beta, Student's t, χ².
Joint f(x,y): distribution of (X,Y) together. Marginal: f_X(x) = Σ_y f(x,y) (or ∫ f(x,y)dy). Conditional: f(y|x) = f(x,y)/f_X(x).
X and Y are independent if P(X∈A, Y∈B) = P(X∈A)P(Y∈B) for all A, B; equivalently f(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y).
Independent and identically distributed: independent random variables that all have the same distribution. The standard model of a random sample.
E[X] = Σ x f(x) (or ∫ x f(x)dx): the mean, or long-run average, of X. It is linear: E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c, and E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] if X, Y are independent.
Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²] = E[X²] − (E[X])². Measures spread; Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X).
X̄ = (1/n)ΣXi and S² = (1/(n−1))Σ(Xi − X̄)². Unbiased estimators of E[X] and Var(X) for IID data.
Cov(X,Y) = E[(X−μ_X)(Y−μ_Y)]. Correlation ρ = Cov(X,Y)/(σ_X σ_Y) lies in [−1, 1] and measures linear dependence.
For a random vector X with mean μ and covariance matrix Σ: E[AX + b] = Aμ + b and Cov(AX + b) = AΣAᵀ. Σ is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
E[Y|X=x] = ∫ y f(y|x)dy: the mean of Y given X. E[Y|X] is itself a random variable, and the law of total expectation says E[E[Y|X]] = E[Y].
Fully determined by mean μ and covariance Σ. Linear transformations are Normal (AX+b ~ N(Aμ+b, AΣAᵀ)); marginals and conditionals are Normal; uncorrelated components are independent.
For X ≥ 0 and t > 0: P(X ≥ t) ≤ E[X]/t.
P(|X − μ| ≥ t) ≤ σ²/t², where μ = E[X] and σ² = Var(X).
Xn → X in probability if for every ε > 0, P(|Xn − X| > ε) → 0 as n → ∞.
Xn converges in distribution to X if F_n(t) → F(t) at every point t where F is continuous.
For IID Xi with finite mean μ, the sample mean X̄n converges in probability to μ.
For IID Xi with mean μ and variance σ², √n(X̄n − μ)/σ converges in distribution to N(0,1); so X̄n is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) for large n.
A set of distributions (or densities) assumed to contain the one that generated the data. Parametric if indexed by finitely many parameters, nonparametric otherwise.
A function of the data, θ̂n = g(X1,…,Xn), used to estimate a quantity of interest. It is itself a random variable.
Bias = E[θ̂] − θ. An estimator is consistent if θ̂n converges in probability to the true θ as n grows.
The sampling distribution is the distribution of an estimator over repeated samples; the standard error se(θ̂) is its standard deviation.
MSE = E[(θ̂ − θ)²] = bias² + Var(θ̂).

A random set Cn that contains the true parameter with probability at least 1−α for all parameter values. In 1D, a confidence interval. The 1−α refers to coverage over repeated experiments, not the probability that θ lies in this particular interval.
The empirical CDF F̂n(x) = (1/n)Σ I(Xi ≤ x), which puts mass 1/n on each observation. It converges uniformly to the true CDF (Glivenko–Cantelli) and the DKW inequality bounds its error.
Estimates a summary T(F) of the CDF by T(F̂n). Examples: sample mean, sample variance and sample quantiles.
θ̂ ± z_{α/2}·se, valid when θ̂ is approximately Normal. For 95% confidence, θ̂ ± 1.96·se.

Estimates standard errors and confidence intervals by repeatedly resampling the data with replacement (i.e. sampling from F̂n), recomputing the statistic each time and using the spread of the replicates.
Two approximations: F̂n ≈ F, and simulation error from using finite B resamples. It can fail for non-smooth statistics (e.g. the maximum), heavy tails, dependent data and very small samples.
θ̂ ± z_{α/2}·se_boot, where se_boot is the standard deviation of the bootstrap replicates.
(θ*_{α/2}, θ*_{1−α/2}): the α/2 and 1−α/2 quantiles of the bootstrap replicates.
Uses the bootstrap distribution of θ̂* − θ̂ to approximate that of θ̂ − θ: C = (2θ̂ − θ*_{1−α/2}, 2θ̂ − θ*_{α/2}).
A family of distributions {f(x;θ) : θ ∈ Θ} indexed by a finite number of parameters θ.
Set the first k population moments (functions of θ) equal to the corresponding sample moments and solve for θ. Simple and consistent, but not always efficient.
The likelihood is L(θ) = ∏ f(Xi;θ), viewed as a function of θ. The MLE θ̂ is the value that maximizes L(θ), equivalently the log-likelihood ℓ(θ).
Maximize the log-likelihood: where possible set the score (derivative of ℓ) to zero and solve analytically, otherwise use numerical optimization.
Iterative algorithms (e.g. Newton's method, gradient ascent) used to maximize or minimize a function when there is no closed-form solution. May get stuck in local optima.
Update θ ← θ + η∇ℓ(θ) with step size η. Stochastic gradient methods use the gradient on a random minibatch of data at each step: a cheap, noisy estimate of the full gradient.

column1: Properties of the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE)
column2: Under regularity conditions the MLE is consistent, equivariant, asymptotically Normal and asymptotically optimal.
The MLE θ̂n converges in probability to the true parameter θ as n → ∞.
If θ̂ is the MLE of θ, then g(θ̂) is the MLE of g(θ).
(θ̂ − θ)/se converges in distribution to N(0,1), where se ≈ 1/√(nI(θ)).
For large n, the MLE has the smallest asymptotic variance among well-behaved estimators (it attains the Cramér–Rao bound asymptotically); it is asymptotically efficient.
θ̂ ± z_{α/2}·ŝe, where ŝe = 1/√(nI(θ̂)) is based on the Fisher information.
I(θ) = Var(score) = −E[∂² log f(X;θ)/∂θ²]. Measures the curvature of the log-likelihood (how much information the data carry about θ); for n IID observations In(θ) = nI(θ).
If τ = g(θ) with g'(θ) ≠ 0, then se(τ̂) ≈ |g'(θ̂)|·se(θ̂) and τ̂ is approximately Normal. Used to get standard errors and intervals for transformed parameters.

column1: Multiparameter models and the Fisher information matrix
column2: I_jk(θ) = −E[∂²ℓ/∂θ_j∂θ_k]. The covariance of the MLE is approximately the inverse of the Fisher information matrix; the multivariate delta method uses the gradient of g.
A statistic T(X) is sufficient for θ if the distribution of the data given T does not depend on θ: T captures all information about θ. Checked via the factorization theorem.

column1: Cross-entropy loss and maximum likelihood estimation
column2: Minimizing the cross-entropy between the empirical data distribution and the model is the same as maximizing the log-likelihood; e.g. classification cross-entropy loss is the negative log-likelihood.

column1: EM algorithm for latent variable models
column2: Iteratively maximizes the likelihood when some variables are latent. E-step: compute expected complete-data log-likelihood under the current posterior of the latents. M-step: maximize it over θ. The likelihood never decreases, but it may converge to a local optimum.
The null hypothesis H0 (default claim) and the alternative H1. Testing asks whether the data provide enough evidence to reject H0.
Rejecting H0 when H0 is true (false positive).
Failing to reject H0 when H0 is false (false negative).
Size = sup over θ in H0 of P_θ(reject H0). A test has level α if its size is at most α.
The probability, assuming H0 is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed; equivalently the smallest α at which the test rejects. It is not the probability that H0 is true.
β(θ) = P_θ(reject H0). The probability of correctly rejecting H0 when the alternative holds; equals 1 − P(Type II error).
Reject H0: θ = θ0 if |W| = |θ̂ − θ0|/ŝe > z_{α/2}. Relies on the asymptotic Normality of the estimator.

Builds the null distribution by permuting labels/data (valid when the data are exchangeable under H0); the p-value is the fraction of permutations with a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one.
Statistic λ = 2 log[sup_Θ L(θ) / sup_Θ0 L(θ)]. Under H0 it is approximately χ² with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in numbers of free parameters (Wilks' theorem).
Running many tests at once inflates the chance of at least one false positive, so corrections are needed.
Reject H_i if p_i < α/m (m = number of tests). Controls the family-wise error rate at α; conservative.
FDR = E[number of false rejections / number of rejections]: the expected proportion of rejected hypotheses that are false discoveries.
Sort p-values p_(1) ≤ … ≤ p_(m), find the largest i with p_(i) ≤ iα/m, and reject all hypotheses up to i. Controls the FDR at α (under independence or positive dependence).
p-values modified for multiple testing so that comparing them to α gives the desired error control (e.g. Bonferroni: min(m·p, 1)).

column1: Strengths and weaknesses of null-hypothesis significance testing
column2: Strengths: simple, standardized, controls error rates. Weaknesses: p-values often misinterpreted; statistical significance ≠ practical importance; depends heavily on n; encourages yes/no thinking and p-hacking; gives no effect size or probability of hypotheses.
The prior π(θ) encodes beliefs about θ before seeing data. The posterior p(θ|x) ∝ L(θ)π(θ) is the updated belief after observing data.
Choose a model and prior, observe data, compute the posterior with Bayes' theorem, then summarize it and make predictions or decisions from it.

column1: Posterior summaries: point estimates and credible intervals
column2: Point estimates: posterior mean, median, or mode (MAP). A 1−α credible interval C satisfies P(θ ∈ C | data) = 1−α.
Informative, weakly informative, noninformative/flat, conjugate (posterior is in the same family as the prior) and improper (does not integrate to 1).
L(θ, θ̂) measures the cost of estimating θ by θ̂. Examples: squared error, absolute error, 0–1 loss.
R(θ, θ̂) = E_θ[L(θ, θ̂(X))]: expected loss over repeated data sets. The Bayes risk averages R over the prior.
A Bayes estimator minimizes the Bayes risk (equivalently the posterior expected loss; the posterior mean under squared error). A minimax estimator minimizes the worst-case risk sup_θ R(θ, θ̂).
An estimator is inadmissible if another estimator has risk no larger for all θ and strictly smaller for some θ; otherwise it is admissible.
Models the mean of Y as a linear function of predictors: Y = β0 + β1X1 + … + ε, with E[ε] = 0.

column1: Least squares estimation and connection to MLE
column2: Choose β to minimize Σ(Yi − Xiᵀβ)². This coincides with the MLE when the errors are IID Normal.
Y = Xβ + ε with design matrix X. The least squares estimate is β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY.
βj is the expected change in Y for a one-unit increase in Xj with all other predictors held fixed. It describes association, not necessarily causation.
Product terms such as X1·X2 that let the effect of one predictor depend on the value of another.

column1: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for parameters
column2: CI: β̂j ± t·se(β̂j). The t-test of H0: βj = 0 uses t = β̂j/se(β̂j).
Choosing which predictors to include, balancing fit against complexity and overfitting.
Expected squared prediction error on new data. The training error underestimates it, so it must be estimated (Cp, AIC, BIC, cross-validation).
An estimate of prediction risk: training RSS plus a penalty 2kσ̂² for the k fitted parameters. Lower is better.
Akaike information criterion: −2ℓ(θ̂) + 2k (k = number of parameters). Penalizes complexity; aims at good prediction.
Bayesian information criterion: −2ℓ(θ̂) + k·log n. A stronger penalty than AIC, so it prefers simpler models.
Split data into folds; repeatedly fit on some folds and measure prediction error on the held-out fold; average the errors. Leave-one-out is the extreme case.
Greedy variable selection. Forward: start empty and add the predictor that most improves the criterion. Backward: start with all predictors and drop the least useful one.
Coefficients obtained after scaling predictors to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, making their magnitudes comparable across predictors.
Assumptions: linearity, independent errors, constant variance (homoscedasticity), Normal errors. Residual plots (e.g. residuals vs fitted values) reveal curvature, non-constant variance and outliers.
For binary outcomes: logit P(Y=1|x) = log(p/(1−p)) = β0 + βᵀx. Fit by maximum likelihood; coefficients are log odds ratios.
Constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior; the (correlated) draws approximate posterior expectations. Examples: Metropolis–Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo/NUTS.
Plots of sampled values against iteration for each chain. Healthy chains look stationary ("fuzzy caterpillar") and multiple chains overlap.
Convergence diagnostic comparing between-chain and within-chain variance across multiple chains. Values close to 1 (e.g. < 1.01) indicate convergence.
The number of independent draws that would carry the same information as the autocorrelated MCMC sample. Low ESS means noisy estimates.
PyMC is a Python probabilistic programming library: declare priors and the likelihood in a model context, then run MCMC (NUTS by default) to sample the posterior.
Simulate data from the prior and likelihood before fitting, to check that the priors imply plausible data.
Summarizing and checking posterior samples: means, credible intervals, posterior plots and posterior predictive checks.
Comparing models by marginal likelihood (Bayes factors) or by out-of-sample predictive performance (ELPD, LOO).
Setting where the true model is assumed to be among the candidates. Models are compared by the Bayes factor, the ratio of marginal likelihoods p(D|M1)/p(D|M2).
Setting where the true model is not among the candidates. Models are compared by predictive accuracy: ELPD, the expected log predictive density on new data.
Estimates ELPD from leave-one-out predictive densities, efficiently approximated from a single fit with Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO).
Normal likelihood (known variance) with a Normal prior on the mean gives a Normal posterior (conjugate). The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean.
Categorical likelihood with a Dirichlet prior on the probabilities gives a Dirichlet posterior: observed counts are added to the prior concentration parameters.
Association does not imply causation: it can arise from confounding or reverse causation. Causal questions ask what happens under an intervention.
do(X = x) denotes intervening to set X to x, which differs from conditioning on observing X = x. In general P(Y | do(X=x)) ≠ P(Y | X=x).
Directed acyclic graphs whose arrows are direct causal effects. They encode conditional independencies and clarify confounders, mediators and colliders.
Each unit has potential outcomes Y(1) and Y(0) under treatment and control, but only one of them is ever observed.
Average causal effect θ = E[Y(1)] − E[Y(0)]. Association α = E[Y|X=1] − E[Y|X=0]. In general θ ≠ α.
Randomly assigning treatment makes X independent of the potential outcomes, so association equals the causal effect.
The causal effect within a subgroup defined by covariates Z: E[Y(1) − Y(0) | Z = z].
θ(x) = E[Y(x)], the mean outcome if everyone were set to X = x. Equals E[Y|X=x] under randomization.
In observational studies treatment is not randomized. A confounder affects both treatment and outcome, biasing naive comparisons.
Assumption that, given measured covariates Z, treatment is independent of the potential outcomes: (Y(0), Y(1)) ⫫ X | Z.

column1: Adjusted treatment effect and adjustment by regression
column2: Under no unmeasured confounding, θ = ∫ (E[Y|X=1,Z=z] − E[Y|X=0,Z=z]) dF(z). Regression adjustment fits Y on X and Z; the coefficient of X estimates the causal effect if the model is right and there is no unmeasured confounding.
A trend in the aggregate data reverses within subgroups because of a confounder. Resolved by using the causal structure to decide whether to adjust for (condition on) the variable.
Nonresponse, dropout, measurement or device failure, data entry errors, censoring, and design choices.
How the probability of missingness relates to the data: MCAR, MAR or MNAR.
Missingness is independent of both observed and unobserved data.
Missingness depends only on observed data, not on the missing values themselves.
Missingness depends on the unobserved values themselves, even after accounting for observed data.
The missingness mechanism can be ignored for inference (e.g. MAR and mechanism parameters distinct from model parameters), so we need not model it.
Drop all rows with any missing values. Unbiased under MCAR but wasteful, and potentially biased otherwise.
Fill in missing values (mean, regression, hot-deck, multiple imputation). Single imputation understates uncertainty; multiple imputation propagates it.
Weight observed cases by the inverse of their probability of being observed so they represent the full sample. Works under MAR.
Specify a joint model for data (and possibly missingness) and use likelihood or Bayesian inference, treating missing values as latent (e.g. with EM).
Conclusions are limited by how the data were collected; no analysis can rescue badly collected data.
Planning how to select a sample from a population so that population quantities can be estimated accurately.
Target population: everyone we want to learn about. Sampling frame: the list from which the sample is actually drawn. A mismatch causes coverage error.
Simple random, stratified, cluster and systematic sampling (probability samples), versus convenience sampling (non-probability).
The same respondents are surveyed repeatedly over time. Good for tracking change, but subject to attrition and conditioning effects.
Nonrespondents often differ systematically from respondents, leading to nonresponse bias.
Weighting, poststratification, raking or imputation to correct for nonresponse and for sample/population imbalances.
Wording, order and response options influence answers (leading or double-barreled questions, social desirability bias).
Randomized assignment, control groups, replication and blinding, so that treatment effects can be isolated.
Goals: valid causal inference and precision. Pitfalls: confounding, small samples, noncompliance, lack of blinding, multiple comparisons, p-hacking.
Each participant receives all conditions. Removes between-person variability, but risks carryover and order effects.
Each participant receives only one condition. No carryover effects, but needs more participants.
Cross all levels of several factors to estimate main effects and interactions. Fractional factorial designs run only a subset of the combinations when there are many factors.
Determines the sample size needed to detect an effect of a given size with a chosen power (e.g. 80%) at significance level α.

column1: Type S and Type M errors
column2: Type S (sign): the estimate has the wrong sign. Type M (magnitude): the effect size is exaggerated. Both are common among significant results from underpowered studies.
